questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Converting radians to degrees
questions.learningObjective: explain why one turn carries both a radian and a degree measure
questions.stem: A graph shows a complete circle labelled 360 degrees at the rim and 2*pi radians at the same mark. Explain why these two labels describe the same sweep, and how to convert between them.

answer.exemplar: A radian is defined as the angle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius, so a full sweep of a circle of radius r has an arc length of 2*pi*r, and the angle that produces that arc is 2*pi radians. The degree scale is older and simply marks a full turn as 360 parts, so the same physical sweep carries both labels. Because a half turn is pi radians and also 180 degrees, the two scales are locked together by the ratio 180 over pi, and that ratio converts any angle in either direction. This is why a graph with a degree rim and a radian axis can be read in either scale: the marks sit at fixed positions and only the number attached to each mark changes. The factor is fixed because both scales agree on what a half turn and a full turn are.

questions.explanation: A radian measures an angle by the arc it cuts off, so a full turn of a circle is 2*pi radians, while the degree scale marks that same turn as 360. The ratio 180 over pi links the scales.
questions.hint: Start from the definition of one radian.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Arc length from a central angle in radians
questions.learningObjective: explain the definition of a radian through the arc length formula
questions.stem: A graph marks an arc whose length equals the radius of the circle. Explain what that means for the angle, and how it produces the arc length formula.

answer.exemplar: An angle of one radian is defined as the angle that cuts off an arc whose length equals the radius of the circle, so the arc and the radius are the same length by construction. Multiplying the radius by the number of radians in the angle therefore counts how many radii fit along the arc, which is exactly the arc length, and that is the formula s = r*theta. The reason the angle has to be measured in radians is now obvious: the count of radii is only equal to the radian measure, so a degree number inserted in that slot is not a count of anything and the arc comes out too large. The same idea, applied to a full turn of 2*pi radians, explains why a whole circle has circumference 2*pi*r, which is the limit of the formula when the angle is 2*pi.

questions.explanation: One radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius, so multiplying the radius by the radian angle counts the radii along the arc. That is why the formula needs radians.
questions.hint: Start from the definition of one radian.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Sector area from a central angle in radians
questions.learningObjective: explain the one half in the sector area formula
questions.stem: A graph shows a shaded sector of a circle. Explain where the one half in the sector area formula comes from, and why the angle must be in radians.

answer.exemplar: The sector takes a fraction theta over 2*pi of the whole disk, since a full turn of 2*pi radians fills the disk, so its area is that fraction of pi*r squared. Multiplying pi*r squared by theta over 2*pi cancels the pi and leaves one half of r squared times theta, which is where the one half comes from: it is the price of dividing by the turn measure. The same cancellation is why the angle has to be in radians. Measured in degrees, the fraction of the disk would be theta over 360, and the area would come out as pi*r squared times theta over 360, a different formula that still works but carries pi around. Written in radians the formula becomes short, and the quick checks, a quarter disk and a quarter of the rim, fall out immediately.

questions.explanation: The sector covers the fraction theta over 2*pi of the disk, so multiplying by pi*r squared cancels the pi and leaves one half r squared theta. That is also why the angle must be in radians.
questions.hint: Compare the sector with the whole disk.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Reading coordinates on the unit circle
questions.learningObjective: explain how unit circle coordinates relate to sine and cosine
questions.stem: A graph of the unit circle shows a marked point. Explain how the coordinates of that point relate to the sine and cosine of the angle it marks.

answer.exemplar: On the unit circle the radius is 1, and dropping a perpendicular from the marked point to the x axis builds a right triangle whose hypotenuse is that radius. The horizontal side is the adjacent leg, so the cosine of the angle, which is adjacent over hypotenuse, is exactly the horizontal coordinate, and the vertical side is the opposite leg, so the sine is exactly the vertical coordinate. That is why the coordinates of any point on the unit circle are the ordered pair cosine and sine of the marked angle. It also explains the signs: a point in the second quadrant has a negative horizontal coordinate and a positive vertical one, and in the third quadrant both are negative. Since the radius is 1, the hypotenuse never changes, and the two ratios are simply the two legs of the triangle.

questions.explanation: Dropping a perpendicular from the point to the axis gives a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, so the horizontal coordinate is the cosine and the vertical coordinate is the sine of the marked angle.
questions.hint: Draw the right triangle inside the circle.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Trigonometric ratios in a right triangle
questions.learningObjective: explain how to read the trigonometric ratios off a graph
questions.stem: A graph shows a right triangle with a marked angle. Explain how to read the three ratios from that graph and why the hypotenuse is the denominator in two of them.

answer.exemplar: Once the right angle, the marked angle and the sides are identified on the graph, the three ratios follow from where each side sits relative to the marked angle. The side opposite the marked angle is the one across from it, the side touching it and the right angle is the adjacent leg, and the side touching the right angle is the hypotenuse. The sine divides the opposite leg by the hypotenuse and the cosine divides the adjacent leg by the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is the denominator in both because it is the common reference for every angle of the triangle. The tangent is different: it divides the two legs, so it needs no hypotenuse and is the only ratio that can exceed 1. Reading a graph with care about which side is opposite is the whole task, and mislabelling that side is what produces the wrong answer.

questions.explanation: Opposite and adjacent are read from where the sides sit relative to the marked angle, and the hypotenuse touches the right angle. That is why the sine and cosine both divide by it.
questions.hint: Identify the sides by their position, not their size.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The 30-60-90 triangle ratios
questions.learningObjective: explain why the 30-60-90 side ratios are fixed
questions.stem: A graph of a 30-60-90 triangle is labelled with a 30 degree angle and a 60 degree angle. Explain why the side lengths of this triangle can be read off so easily, and how the ratios are used.

answer.exemplar: The 30-60-90 triangle is the one right triangle whose angles pin down its side ratios, because the 30 degree angle comes from bisecting an equilateral triangle and the 60 degree angle from the same construction. Bisecting an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives a right triangle with a hypotenuse of 2, a short leg of 1 and a long leg of root 3, and every other 30-60-90 triangle is a scaled copy of it. That is why the sides always run in the ratio 1 to root 3 to 2, with the short leg exactly half the hypotenuse. On a graph this makes the triangle the quickest one to measure: read the short leg, then multiply by root 3 for the long leg and by 2 for the hypotenuse, or work backwards from the hypotenuse by halving it. The same ratios also give the familiar unit circle values, since a 30-60-90 triangle drawn inside the unit circle has a hypotenuse of 1.

questions.explanation: The triangle comes from bisecting an equilateral triangle, so its sides are always in the ratio 1 to root 3 to 2. That makes the short leg half the hypotenuse and the long leg root 3 times the short leg.
questions.hint: Think about where the 30 degree angle comes from.
